subChunks.title: Combining Conditions — AND, OR, NOT
subChunks.hookHtml: One WHERE condition is rarely enough. "Apprentices who are Mages and have over 4000 XP" is a question with two filters joined by AND. The boolean operators — AND, OR, NOT — are how you stack conditions. Mix them carelessly and you'll get the wrong answer without ever seeing an error.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The three boolean operators

-- AND — both must be true:
SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE rank = 'Mage' AND xp > 4000;

-- OR — at least one must be true:
SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept';

-- NOT — invert the next condition:
SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE NOT rank = 'Novice';

Operator precedence — the trap

AND binds tighter than OR. This:

WHERE rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept' AND xp > 4000

does not mean "a Mage or Adept who has over 4000 XP." It means "a Mage, OR (an Adept with over 4000 XP)." An Apprentice-rank Mage with 100 XP would still match, because the first half — rank = 'Mage' — is satisfied.

The fix is parentheses. Always.

-- The bug:
WHERE rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept' AND xp > 4000

-- The fix:
WHERE (rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept') AND xp > 4000

If you ever doubt how SQL will group your conditions, parenthesise. Engines never punish you for being explicit.

De Morgan's laws — for when NOT meets a compound

If you ever need to negate a compound condition, two algebraic identities help:

NOT (A AND B)  ≡  (NOT A) OR  (NOT B)
NOT (A OR  B)  ≡  (NOT A) AND (NOT B)

So "NOT (a Mage with over 4000 XP)" = "NOT a Mage, OR not over 4000 XP." These laws come up surprisingly often when writing exclusion filters.

Read your conditions out loud

Best discipline: when you write a WHERE clause, read it back to yourself in plain English. "Rank is Mage and xp is greater than 4000." If the English makes sense, the SQL probably does too. If you can't say it cleanly, the conditions are tangled and you should add parentheses or split the query.

storyBeats.text: Cipher slides three new requests across the desk — apprentices needing answers from the archives.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Today's questions are compound. The first runner wants "all Mages with over 4000 XP." The second wants "all Mages or Adepts." The third wants "everyone who is not a Novice." Each is built from a primitive condition plus a connector — AND, OR, NOT. Simple in isolation. Treacherous when mixed.

storyBeats.speaker: The trap of mixed AND/OR
storyBeats.text:
-- WRONG — "Mages, OR Adepts with over 4000 XP":
SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept' AND xp > 4000;

-- This catches every Mage regardless of XP, plus only high-XP Adepts.
-- Probably not what was asked.

-- RIGHT — "a Mage or Adept who has over 4000 XP":
SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE (rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept') AND xp > 4000;

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The reason: AND binds tighter than OR. The engine groups rank = 'Adept' AND xp > 4000 first, then ORs the result with rank = 'Mage'. Parentheses override the default — and even when they would not change the result, they prevent the next reader from misinterpreting your query.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Practical rule: if you have both AND and OR in the same WHERE clause, parenthesise. Always. The cost of an extra pair of brackets is zero. The cost of a wrong answer in a production report is — well, you don't want to find out.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 The parentheses test

Cipher needs the names of apprentices who are Mages OR Adepts AND who have more than 1,000 XP. Both conditions must hold — i.e. they must be either a Mage or an Adept, AND they must have more than 1,000 XP. Get the parentheses right.

Reference data has 5 apprentices now (Eleanor was added):

id | name    | rank        | xp
---+---------+-------------+------
 1 | Alice   | Apprentice  | 1200
 2 | Bjorn   | Adept       | 2400
 3 | Cassia  | Mage        | 4800
 4 | Dorian  | Novice      |   80
 5 | Eleanor | Adept       |  500

Expected: Bjorn (2400) and Cassia (4800) — both qualify. Eleanor is an Adept but has only 500 XP. Alice is an Apprentice. Dorian is a Novice with 80 XP.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- Mages OR Adepts AND xp > 1000.
-- Mind the parentheses!
SELECT name
FROM apprentices
WHERE
  -- your condition here
;

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns exactly 2 rows
guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE apprentices (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, rank TEXT NOT NULL, xp INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES (1,'Alice','Apprentice',1200),(2,'Bjorn','Adept',2400),(3,'Cassia','Mage',4800),(4,'Dorian','Novice',80),(5,'Eleanor','Adept',500);

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns Bjorn and Cassia (excludes low-XP Adept Eleanor)
guidedPracticeTests.expectedQuery: SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE (rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept') AND xp > 1000

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo Challenge — NOT a Novice

Same data. Write a query that returns the names of all apprentices whose rank is not 'Novice'. Use NOT or <> — your choice.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a teammate why "WHERE rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept' AND xp > 4000" gives a different answer than "WHERE (rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept') AND xp > 4000". Use the apprentices ledger to walk through which rows each query returns and why.

questions.questionHtml: Which boolean operator binds tightest in SQL — i.e. is evaluated before the others when no parentheses are used?
questions.explanationHtml: Standard precedence is NOT > AND > OR. NOT binds to its single operand first; AND groups before OR. The practical takeaway: use parentheses whenever you mix AND with OR.

questions.questionHtml:
Given the apprentices table from the lesson, what does this query return?

SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept' AND xp > 4000;
options: Cassia (every Mage; no Adept has xp>4000)
Nobody (no row satisfies all three primitive conditions)
Bjorn (the only Adept with high XP)
questions.correctAnswer: Cassia (every Mage; no Adept has xp>4000)
questions.explanationHtml: AND binds first, so the engine groups it as rank='Mage' OR (rank='Adept' AND xp>4000). Cassia is a Mage → matches the first half. Bjorn is an Adept but xp is 2400, so the AND part fails. Result: just Cassia.

questions.questionHtml: Which query correctly returns "all apprentices who are NOT a Novice and NOT an Apprentice"?
questions.explanationHtml: "Not Novice AND not Apprentice" excludes both. Option 3 (using OR) is true for every row — every rank is at least one of "not Novice" or "not Apprentice". Option 4 is true for every row, since no row has rank equal to both at once. By De Morgan, rank<>'Novice' AND rank<>'Apprentice' equals NOT (rank='Novice' OR rank='Apprentice').

questions.questionHtml:
A junior wants "users who are admins or who have premium accounts, and have logged in this week." They write:

WHERE role = 'admin' OR plan = 'premium' AND last_login > :week_start

Why is this likely a bug?
options: AND binds tighter than OR, so the engine reads it as 'role=admin OR (plan=premium AND last_login>...)' — every admin matches regardless of login activity
OR is not a valid keyword in SQL; it should be ||
Three conditions can never be combined in one WHERE clause without subqueries
The query is correct as written; AND and OR have equal precedence in SQL
questions.correctAnswer: AND binds tighter than OR, so the engine reads it as 'role=admin OR (plan=premium AND last_login>...)' — every admin matches regardless of login activity
questions.explanationHtml: Classic AND/OR precedence trap. The fix is parentheses: WHERE (role = 'admin' OR plan = 'premium') AND last_login > :week_start. This is one of the most common production SQL bugs — it doesn't error, it just returns wrong data, often silently for months until somebody notices.

subChunks.title: Patterns and Lists — IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, NULL
subChunks.hookHtml: You have =, <, >. They're powerful but verbose. Real-world filters reach for IN (membership), BETWEEN (range), LIKE (pattern), and IS NULL (absence). Each one collapses ten lines of equivalent ORs into one clear expression.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
IN — value is one of these

-- Long-hand:
WHERE rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept' OR rank = 'Archmage'

-- Equivalent, idiomatic:
WHERE rank IN ('Mage', 'Adept', 'Archmage')

-- Negated:
WHERE rank NOT IN ('Novice', 'Apprentice')

IN works with any number of values, and most powerfully with a subquery — but we'll meet subqueries later.

BETWEEN — value falls in a range (inclusive)

-- xp from 1000 to 4000, inclusive of both ends:
WHERE xp BETWEEN 1000 AND 4000

-- Equivalent:
WHERE xp >= 1000 AND xp <= 4000

BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends. BETWEEN 1 AND 5 includes 1 and 5. If you mean exclusive, write the explicit comparison.

LIKE — pattern matching for strings

-- Names starting with 'A':
WHERE name LIKE 'A%'

-- Names ending in 'a':
WHERE name LIKE '%a'

-- Names containing 'rc' anywhere:
WHERE name LIKE '%rc%'

-- Five-letter names:
WHERE name LIKE '_____'

-- Names where the second letter is 'l':
WHERE name LIKE '_l%'

Two wildcards: % means "any number of characters (including zero)," _ means "exactly one character." Case sensitivity is engine-dependent — PostgreSQL is case-sensitive, MySQL is not by default.

NULL — the value that isn't

NULL means "unknown" or "absent" — not zero, not empty string. NULL infects comparisons:

-- These never return rows where the column is NULL:
WHERE col = 'something'
WHERE col <> 'something'
WHERE col IS NOT 'something'   -- WRONG: 'IS' only works with NULL/TRUE/FALSE

-- The correct way to test for NULL:
WHERE col IS NULL
WHERE col IS NOT NULL

This is the most common SQL bug for newcomers: writing WHERE col = NULL. It's not a syntax error; it just never returns any row, because NULL = NULL evaluates to NULL, not TRUE. Use IS NULL, always.

Combining everything

-- Apprentices whose name starts with 'A' or 'B',
-- have between 1000 and 5000 xp,
-- and whose rank is one we care about:
SELECT name, rank, xp
FROM apprentices
WHERE (name LIKE 'A%' OR name LIKE 'B%')
  AND xp BETWEEN 1000 AND 5000
  AND rank IN ('Apprentice', 'Adept', 'Mage');

storyBeats.text: Cipher pulls a new ledger from a tall shelf — this one has a column you haven't seen before, with several blank entries.

storyBeats.speaker: The quests ledger — note the blanks
storyBeats.text:
id | title              | xp_reward | difficulty   | completed_by
---+--------------------+-----------+--------------+--------------
 1 | Tame the Slime     |   100     | Foundation   | 1
 2 | Decode the Glyph   |   180     | Foundation   | 2
 3 | Forge the Blade    |   400     | Practitioner | NULL
 4 | Slay the Drake     |  1200     | Expert       | NULL
 5 | Brew the Elixir    |   220     | NULL         | 3

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Look closely. Some quests have no completed_by — nobody has finished them. Some have no difficulty — the Headmaster hasn't decided yet. These blanks are NULL: not zero, not empty text. Unknown. Absent. Different from any value you can write down.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And NULL is treacherous. WHERE completed_by = NULL looks reasonable. It returns nothing. Always. Because comparing anything to NULL with = produces NULL, not TRUE. To find rows where a column has no value, you write WHERE completed_by IS NULL. It is a special syntax for a special case.

storyBeats.speaker: Filtering with IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL
Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Each operator collapses what would otherwise be a long compound expression. IN replaces a chain of ORs. BETWEEN replaces a pair of inequalities. LIKE handles partial matches. IS NULL is the only correct way to ask about the absence of a value. Practise them until they're as natural as =.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Mid-tier rewards

Cipher needs the titles of all quests with rewards between 200 and 500 XP, inclusive. Use BETWEEN — it's the idiomatic operator for inclusive ranges.

Reference data:

id | title              | xp_reward | difficulty   | completed_by
---+--------------------+-----------+--------------+--------------
 1 | Tame the Slime     |   100     | Foundation   | 1
 2 | Decode the Glyph   |   180     | Foundation   | 2
 3 | Forge the Blade    |   400     | Practitioner | NULL
 4 | Slay the Drake     |  1200     | Expert       | NULL
 5 | Brew the Elixir    |   220     | NULL         | 3

Expected: Forge the Blade (400) and Brew the Elixir (220). Tame the Slime (100) and Decode the Glyph (180) are below the range; Slay the Drake (1200) is above.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- Titles of quests with reward between 200 and 500 (inclusive).
SELECT title
FROM quests
WHERE
  -- BETWEEN ... AND ... ?
;

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns exactly 2 rows
guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE quests (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, xp_reward INTEGER NOT NULL, difficulty TEXT, completed_by INTEGER); INSERT INTO quests VALUES (1,'Tame the Slime',100,'Foundation',1),(2,'Decode the Glyph',180,'Foundation',2),(3,'Forge the Blade',400,'Practitioner',NULL),(4,'Slay the Drake',1200,'Expert',NULL),(5,'Brew the Elixir',220,NULL,3);

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns Forge the Blade and Brew the Elixir
guidedPracticeTests.expectedQuery: SELECT title FROM quests WHERE xp_reward BETWEEN 200 AND 500

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo Challenge — Unfinished business

Same quests table. Write a query that returns the titles of all quests nobody has completed yet — i.e. completed_by IS NULL. Order doesn't matter.

Hint: remember that = NULL never matches anything. Use IS NULL.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why `WHERE completed_by = NULL` always returns zero rows, even when the table contains rows where completed_by is null. Then explain when to use `IN`, `BETWEEN`, and `LIKE` instead of stacking equality checks with OR.

questions.questionHtml: How do you correctly test whether a column completed_by has no value (i.e. is NULL)?
questions.explanationHtml: NULL never equals anything — not even another NULL — when compared with =. The special IS NULL / IS NOT NULL syntax is the only correct way to test for absence.

questions.questionHtml:
Using the quests table, which titles does this query return?

SELECT title FROM quests WHERE xp_reward BETWEEN 200 AND 500;
options: Forge the Blade, Brew the Elixir
Forge the Blade, Slay the Drake, Brew the Elixir
questions.correctAnswer: Forge the Blade, Brew the Elixir
questions.explanationHtml: BETWEEN 200 AND 500 is inclusive on both ends. Forge the Blade has xp=400, Brew the Elixir has xp=220. Tame the Slime (100) and Decode the Glyph (180) are below 200; Slay the Drake (1200) is above 500.

questions.questionHtml: Which expression is equivalent to WHERE rank IN ('Mage', 'Adept', 'Archmage')?
options: WHERE rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept' OR rank = 'Archmage'
WHERE rank = 'Mage' AND rank = 'Adept' AND rank = 'Archmage'
questions.correctAnswer: WHERE rank = 'Mage' OR rank = 'Adept' OR rank = 'Archmage'
questions.explanationHtml: IN is shorthand for a chain of OR-equality checks. Useful both for readability and because some engines optimise IN with a hash lookup when the list is large.

questions.questionHtml: An apprentice writes WHERE name LIKE 'a_%'. Which name does this match?
options: Any name starting with 'a' that has at least one more character: 'al', 'alice', 'amber'
Any name containing 'a' followed immediately by '_'
Names ending in 'a' followed by anything
questions.correctAnswer: Any name starting with 'a' that has at least one more character: 'al', 'alice', 'amber'
questions.explanationHtml: In LIKE, _ matches exactly one character; % matches any number (including zero). So 'a_%' = "a, then exactly one character, then any number more." Effectively: any name starting with 'a' and at least 2 characters long. The literal underscore would be matched with the engine's escape mechanism (e.g. LIKE 'a\_%' ESCAPE '\').
